claims.assertion: Only one off-route segment is recorded in the whole trip (F3, 09:32–09:38, +2.96 km), and the total excess over the optimal route is 3.2 km (F1), so the rider's claim that the driver 'went a different way' can only refer to that single 2.96 km segment; the residual 0.24 km is map-matching noise, not a route change.

The driver's reroute is justified as a 'reasonable cause' detour: no traffic incident is recorded near the route in the trip window (F11), and the re-route inference cuts both ways — the only congestion evidence on record is speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard during 08:58–10:01 (F9, F10), which is neither band 1 nor band 2, so under RD-4(b) congestion alone cannot even be argued as a standalone exemption.

Two off-route outcomes must not be conflated: the traffic record shows only moderate flowing traffic (band 4, F9/F10) and fair weather with 0.0 mm rain (F12), so nothing in the accepted traffic evidence rebuts the driver's claim that his GPS selected an alternative corridor during a 49.8-minute trip that ran 21.4 minutes longer than the 28-minute estimate (F2).

The rider never requested a routing change and none was agreed: there are no in-app chat messages at all (F7), so there is no RD-5 consent to rely on for the driver — but equally there is no evidence the driver ignored an instruction from the rider, and the driver's statement (F8) is consistent with the GPS facts rather than contradicted by them.

Any refund on this RydeTAXI trip is limited to the metered distance units of the unexempted segment: the 2.96 km off-route segment (F3) at the applied per-km rate of $1.41/km, which the fare record shows was actually billed as $4.45 for the full 3.2 km excess (F4); the correct computation is 2.96 km × $1.41 = $4.17, so at most $4.17 can be at issue and the $4.45 headline is not defensible in full.

Time components are not refundable under RD-2: the trip was metered with time $12.96 for 49.8 min (F6) and RD-2 refunds only the distance unit of unexempted segments, so no part of the time charge is recoverable even though the trip ran long (F2).

No flag_account should attach to this driver: his 90-day record shows 968 trips, 1 dispute and 0 upheld (route: 0), i.e. he is not a repeated route offender, and the rider's own 90-day history shows 2 disputes with 1 upheld (F13, F14).

weaknesses: F3 is the decisive adverse fact: a single 2.96 km off-route segment running up to 974 m from the optimal route cannot be brushed aside as noise, and RD-1 sets no km or percentage threshold, so the driver's obligation to take the shortest and most direct route is breached on the face of the GPS record.

F11 destroys the only statutory excuse the driver has: with no traffic incident recorded near the route during the trip window, RD-4(a) cannot exempt the segment, and the band 4 readings (F9, F10) are not band 1 or 2, so RD-4(b) cannot rescue it either.

There is no chat at all (F7), so RD-5 mutual agreement is unavailable; the driver's statement (F8, 'I followed my GPS; it rerouted me') is a statement that loses to the GPS record under the system-record rule and is not itself a reasonable cause.

The consequence is that the distance unit of the 2.96 km segment (2.96 km at the $1.41/km rate evidenced by F4 and F6, i.e. $4.17) is likely to be refunded, and the driver's route is therefore recorded as an RD-1 breach rather than a clean trip; F14 shows 0 upheld route disputes today, so this would be his first.

The rider may argue the longer trip (F2, +21.4 min) and the extra time charge in F6 show the deviation was not trivial — but that time element is not recoverable under RD-2, which is a point in our favour, not a defence of the route itself.

This is a RydeTAXI (metered) trip, so distance actually driven enters the fare and the RD-2 mileage formula applies: refund = Σ extra_km of unexempted off-route segments × (fare.distance_fare ÷ fare.distance_km) [F6][RD-2]. The rate derived from the fare record is $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km = $1.41/km [F6][F4][RD-2].

The GPS record shows one off-route segment, 09:32–09:38, driving 2.96 km where the optimal route covers 0.00 km and straying up to 974 m from it [F3]. RD-1 sets no km or percentage threshold, so an unexplained deviation of this size breaches the driver's shortest-and-most-direct-route obligation [F3][RD-1].

No exemption applies to that segment. RD-4(a) fails: the traffic record shows no incident near the route during the trip window [F11][RD-4]. RD-4(b) fails as a standalone exemption: the only speed records are band 4 (30–39 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard, above the band 1/2 range, and RD-4(b) only corroborates (a) — never exempts alone [F9][F10][RD-4]. Fair weather at 0.0 mm rain removes any weather-based reasonable cause [F12][RD-4]. RD-5 also fails: there are no in-app messages at all, so there is no driver request made before leaving the optimal route and no rider agreement predating the 09:32 segment start [F7][F3][RD-5]; the driver's statement that his GPS rerouted him is a statement that yields to the GPS record and is not itself a reasonable cause [F8][F3][RD-1].

RD-3 is not engaged: nothing shows a rider-named stop or rider-requested routing change [F7][F3][RD-3]. Accordingly the 2.96 km segment is an unexempted detour and only its distance unit is refundable [F3][RD-2].

Amount: 2.96 km × $1.41/km = $4.1724, rounded to $4.17 [F3][F6][RD-2]. The billed excess of $4.45 covers 3.2 km, including a ~0.24 km residual (map-matching residue between fare-excess and the segment sum); RD-2 does not refund that residual [F1][F4][F6][RD-2]. The time charge of $12.96 for 49.8 min is not a distance unit and is not recoverable under RD-2, notwithstanding the +21.4 min over-run [F2][F6][RD-2].

RD-6 does not attach a flag: the driver's 90-day profile shows 0 upheld route disputes, so the "repeated breach" precondition for an account flag is unmet; this is his first recorded RD-1 breach [F14][RD-6]. The rider's own profile (2 disputes, 1 upheld, 0 route) does not decide anything here and is not used to establish the detour [F13][RD-1].

events.body:
RIDER: Your fare dispute is settled with a partial refund. The trip was metered, so the extra distance driven counts. GPS showed the driver went 2.96 km off the shortest route between 09:32 and 09:38, with nothing exempting that detour — no traffic incident, no weather issue, no request from you. That segment was refunded at $1.41 per km, giving $4.17. You'll get it as a Ryde voucher. The small leftover distance and the time charge aren't refundable. Nothing further is needed from you.

DRIVER: A route dispute on this trip was decided against you. Records show you left the shortest route from 09:32 to 09:38, covering 2.96 km extra, and none of the allowed exemptions applied — no traffic incident, no weather cause, and no ride request from the rider beforehand. The rider receives a $4.17 Ryde voucher for that distance. This is recorded as your first route breach; because you have no other upheld route disputes in the last 90 days, no flag is placed on your account. Keep to the shortest route unless a valid exemption applies.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows the driver covered 24.7 km against a 21.6 km optimal route, i.e. +3.2 km (+15%) on a metered RydeTAXI trip where distance is billed per km.
One off-route segment ran 09:32–09:38, driving 2.96 km where the optimal route covers 0.00 km and straying up to 974 m from it, which is a route deviation under RD-1.
The deviation was not agreed: there are no in-app messages at all, so no rider consent message exists before the 09:32 segment start, and the driver's own statement only says his GPS rerouted him.

No exemption applies: LTA DataMall records no traffic incident near the route during the trip window, the only speed records are band 4 (30–39 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard, which is not band 1 or 2, and the weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain.

The excess distance was billed at $4.45 (3.2 km × $1.41/km) with no surge (1.0×); the per-km rate derived from F6 is $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km = $1.41/km, so the unexempt segment's 2.96 km × $1.41 = $4.17 is refundable, rounded to the cent.
The driver's 90-day record shows 1 dispute and 0 upheld and no prior upheld route dispute, so the repeated-offender account flag is not triggered here.

weaknesses: The billed excess is $4.45 for 3.2 km (F4) while the single off-route segment adds only 2.96 km (F3); the remaining ~0.24 km residual is not refundable under RD-2, and the driver will argue the whole +3.2 km was one continuous detour.

The driver's statement that his GPS rerouted him (F8) is an attempt to invoke the 'reasonable cause' exception; although F11 shows no incident and F9/F10 are only band 4, the driver may argue the 21.4-minute over-run (F2) shows the alternative was faster, and RD-1's source A7 lets drivers follow GPS for the fastest route.

The 49.8-minute actual duration against a 28-minute estimate (F2) may be blamed on the rider's own late boarding or on general morning congestion rather than the detour, weakening the causal link for the time component (which we do not claim).
The rider's own profile shows 2 disputes in 90 days with 1 upheld (F13), which the driver can use to suggest a pattern of fare complaints.

claims.assertion: Only one off-route segment is recorded in the whole trip (F3, 09:32–09:38, +2.96 km), and the total excess over the optimal route is 3.2 km (F1), so the rider's claim that the driver 'went a different way' can only refer to that single 2.96 km segment; the residual 0.24 km is map-matching noise, not a route change.

The driver's reroute is justified as a 'reasonable cause' detour: no traffic incident is recorded near the route in the trip window (F11), and the re-route inference cuts both ways — the only congestion evidence on record is speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard during 08:58–10:01 (F9, F10), which is neither band 1 nor band 2, so under RD-4(b) congestion alone cannot even be argued as a standalone exemption.

Two off-route outcomes must not be conflated: the traffic record shows only moderate flowing traffic (band 4, F9/F10) and fair weather with 0.0 mm rain (F12), so nothing in the accepted traffic evidence rebuts the driver's claim that his GPS selected an alternative corridor during a 49.8-minute trip that ran 21.4 minutes longer than the 28-minute estimate (F2).

The rider never requested a routing change and none was agreed: there are no in-app chat messages at all (F7), so there is no RD-5 consent to rely on for the driver — but equally there is no evidence the driver ignored an instruction from the rider, and the driver's statement (F8) is consistent with the GPS facts rather than contradicted by them.

Any refund on this RydeTAXI trip is limited to the metered distance units of the unexempted segment: the 2.96 km off-route segment (F3) at the applied per-km rate of $1.41/km, which the fare record shows was actually billed as $4.45 for the full 3.2 km excess (F4); the correct computation is 2.96 km × $1.41 = $4.17, so at most $4.17 can be at issue and the $4.45 headline is not defensible in full.

Time components are not refundable under RD-2: the trip was metered with time $12.96 for 49.8 min (F6) and RD-2 refunds only the distance unit of unexempted segments, so no part of the time charge is recoverable even though the trip ran long (F2).

No flag_account should attach to this driver: his 90-day record shows 968 trips, 1 dispute and 0 upheld (route: 0), i.e. he is not a repeated route offender, and the rider's own 90-day history shows 2 disputes with 1 upheld (F13, F14).

weaknesses: F3 is the decisive adverse fact: a single 2.96 km off-route segment running up to 974 m from the optimal route cannot be brushed aside as noise, and RD-1 sets no km or percentage threshold, so the driver's obligation to take the shortest and most direct route is breached on the face of the GPS record.

F11 destroys the only statutory excuse the driver has: with no traffic incident recorded near the route during the trip window, RD-4(a) cannot exempt the segment, and the band 4 readings (F9, F10) are not band 1 or 2, so RD-4(b) cannot rescue it either.

There is no chat at all (F7), so RD-5 mutual agreement is unavailable; the driver's statement (F8, 'I followed my GPS; it rerouted me') is a statement that loses to the GPS record under the system-record rule and is not itself a reasonable cause.

The consequence is that the distance unit of the 2.96 km segment (2.96 km at the $1.41/km rate evidenced by F4 and F6, i.e. $4.17) is likely to be refunded, and the driver's route is therefore recorded as an RD-1 breach rather than a clean trip; F14 shows 0 upheld route disputes today, so this would be his first.

The rider may argue the longer trip (F2, +21.4 min) and the extra time charge in F6 show the deviation was not trivial — but that time element is not recoverable under RD-2, which is a point in our favour, not a defence of the route itself.

points.response: Accepted on the arithmetic, not on the conclusion: we accept that the refundable distance is the recorded 2.96 km segment (F3), not the 3.2 km headline (F1), and D1 does not dispute that the segment itself was an unexplained deviation.

D2 concedes the decisive point: with no incident recorded near the route in the trip window (F11) and only band 4 speeds, which are neither band 1 nor band 2, on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard (F9, F10), no RD-4 exemption is available and the segment is unexempted under RD-1.

D3 offers no admissible excuse at all: fair weather with 0.0 mm rain (F12) and band 4 traffic (F9, F10) are the opposite of the 'reasonable cause' RD-4 requires, and the longer duration (F2) shows only that the trip took longer, not that the deviation was justified.

D4 misstates the burden: RD-5 requires driver-and-rider agreement reached before leaving the optimal route, and with no chat messages at all (F7) there is no consent on record, while the driver's own statement that his GPS rerouted him (F8) loses to the GPS record of a 974 m-away segment (F3).

We accept the driver's computation: the refundable amount is the unexempted segment's distance unit, 2.96 km × $1.41/km = $4.17 (rate derived from the $34.84 distance charge over 24.7 km in F6, consistent with the $4.45 billed for the 3.2 km excess in F4), not the full $4.45.

Conceded — RD-2 refunds only the distance unit of unexempted segments, so we make no claim against the $12.96 time charge for 49.8 minutes (F6), though the +21.4 minute over-run (F2) remains relevant evidence that the 09:32–09:38 segment was a real detour.
Conceded — the driver's 90-day record of 968 trips with 1 dispute and 0 upheld (F14) does not meet RD-6's repeated-offender condition, so we withdraw any account-flag request.

Conceded as to the arithmetic — the track shows 24.7 km against 21.6 km (F1) and this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, so distance enters the fare (F6) — but the claim's own figures confine the case to the single 2.96 km segment in F3, leaving only the 0.24 km residual, which RD-2 excludes as map-matching residual and which represents no driver conduct at all.

This is the only point on which the driver's case is genuinely exposed: F3 records one segment at 09:32–09:38 adding 2.96 km and straying up to 974 m from the optimal route, and RD-1 sets no km or percentage threshold, so I do not contest that this segment is examined under RD-3/RD-4/RD-5 as a possible unexempted deviation.

The absence of chat (F7) cuts both ways and cannot be converted into an adverse inference: RD-5 only excuses a segment when consent exists, but nothing in F7 or in the driver's statement in F8 shows the rider named a different route or that the driver disregarded an instruction, and F8 is consistent with the GPS record rather than contradicted by it.

Conceded — with no incident near the route in the trip window (F11), the band 4 readings on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard (F9, F10) fall outside band 1/2, and fair weather at 0.0 mm (F12), neither RD-4(a) nor RD-4(b) can exempt the 09:32–09:38 segment.

I adopt the rider's own computation as the ceiling, because it is the only one the policy supports: 2.96 km of unexempted segment (F3) at the rate evidenced by the fare record, $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km = $1.41/km (F6), gives $4.17, and the $4.45 billed figure (F4) covers 3.2 km including the 0.24 km residual that RD-2 expressly does not refund; the driver disputes only that the full 2.96 km should be refunded, since RD-2 refunds the extra_km of the unexempted segment and nothing in F3 fixes the segment's own fault.

The rider's own case disposes of the time component: RD-2 refunds only the distance unit of unexempted segments, so the $12.96 time charge within the $53.17 total (F6) and the 49.8 min actual against the 28 min estimate (F2) generate no refund, and the 21.4-minute over-run stays with the driver only as context, not as money owed.

Agreed, and it matters for the driver: F14 shows 968 trips in 90 days, 1 dispute, 0 upheld and 0 route disputes upheld, so RD-6's 'repeated' precondition (a prior upheld route dispute in the window) is not met and no flag_account should attach to this driver.

Withdrawn: F9 and F10 show only band 4 (30–39 km/h), which is above the band 1/2 range, and F11 shows no incident, so I cannot maintain that a reasonable-cause exemption under RD-4 was established for the 09:32–09:38 segment.

Confirmed as the outer limit of this dispute: the maximum exposure is 2.96 km × $1.41/km = $4.17 (F3, F6), and the balance of the $53.17 total in F6 — base, time and platform components — is unaffected by RD-2.

notices.text: Your fare dispute is settled with a partial refund. The trip was metered, so the extra distance driven counts. GPS showed the driver went 2.96 km off the shortest route between 09:32 and 09:38, with nothing exempting that detour — no traffic incident, no weather issue, no request from you. That segment was refunded at $1.41 per km, giving $4.17. You'll get it as a Ryde voucher. The small leftover distance and the time charge aren't refundable. Nothing further is needed from you.

A route dispute on this trip was decided against you. Records show you left the shortest route from 09:32 to 09:38, covering 2.96 km extra, and none of the allowed exemptions applied — no traffic incident, no weather cause, and no ride request from the rider beforehand. The rider receives a $4.17 Ryde voucher for that distance. This is recorded as your first route breach; because you have no other upheld route disputes in the last 90 days, no flag is placed on your account. Keep to the shortest route unless a valid exemption applies.
